Mostly works in an office with cross-functional teams, using data around supply chains, public services, finance, or operations planning.
Common tools and systems: spreadsheets, SQL, Python or R, optimization solvers, simulation and visualization tools.

Compared with adjacent roles, this occupation is responsible for problem modeling and decision support and is not the same as only producing reports in data analysis or directly making management approvals.
Qualified delivery must demonstrate: a reproducible model, an input data dictionary, scenario comparisons, and decision notes.
U.S. occupational scope and Chinese position titles or credentials need not correspond one-to-one; local requirements are verified by region and employer.

Data scientists mainly do broad data modeling and machine learning; this occupation focuses more on problem modeling and decision support and is not the same as only producing reports in data analysis or directly making management approvals.
Statisticians focus on statistical design and inference, with different occupational tasks and training.
Management analysts lean toward organizational processes and management advice; look at the final output rather than similar titles.
Difference between data scientists and this occupation: operations research analysis focuses more on constraints and optimized decisions.
Choosing data science suits those who prefer exploring predictive models.

paragraphs: Ability judgment can observe supervised modeling, data verification, and decision-note feedback; interests are for exploration only and do not prove model quality or approval authority.
Trials use fictional information only; real tasks must follow qualification and supervision boundaries.

Objective mis-specification: optimizing a single cost while omitting service or fairness constraints.; May make a plan unacceptable in reality. Control: review objectives and limits with the business side.
Data bias: samples are outdated or missing.; May cause model output to mislead decisions. Control: perform quality checks and sensitivity analysis.
Omitted constraints: capacity, regulations, or manual rules are not counted.; May make a plan unexecutable. Control: have the executing party review the model.
Overfitting the solution: the model works only in historical scenarios.; May fail when demand changes. Control: keep stress scenarios and alternatives.
Shared escalation: when equipment, personnel, documentation, or authorization anomalies occur, pause first, document, and hand over to authorized personnel.

Safe exploration uses fictional samples only: compare delivery routes or shifts, write down objectives, constraints, sensitivity, and failure conditions, and do not change real operations. Problem statement: 20 items must be delivered in one day; full shift A has a capacity of 12 items and a cost of 100 yuan, full shift B has a capacity of 10 items and a cost of 90 yuan, each with at most 2 shifts, partial loading is allowed, cost is independent of load, and the number of shifts is a non-negative integer. Compare total cost only across the three cases A+B, 2A, and 2B, list capacity and unused capacity, then change demand to 23 items and re-check; do not call the best of the three candidates a true business global optimum.

BLS lists that a bachelor's degree is usually required; training in mathematics, statistics, computer science, engineering, or a related field helps, and some positions prefer a graduate degree.; Real duties depend on local rules and employer authorization, and changing roles requires training for the target position.

Reference delivery: with 20 items, A+B has capacity 22, cost 190, unused 2; 2A has capacity 24, cost 200, unused 4; 2B has capacity 20, cost 180, unused 0; all three cases are feasible and 2B is the lowest. With demand 23, only 2A with capacity 24 is feasible, costing 200 with unused 1; the original low-cost plan fails. Submit the data dictionary, the feasibility and cost table for the three cases, demand sensitivity, and a note on omitted time windows/routes/fairness limits. Mathematical training does not equal real scheduling approval authority.

career_risk_cards.heading: Main risks for operations research analysts

$join: Analysts, objective setters, and teams affected by resource allocation. Objective context:
May sacrifice service or fairness objectives and make a plan unacceptable. Escalation boundary:

risks.mitigation: Review objectives and limits with the business side.
risks.scenario: Optimizing a single cost while omitting service or fairness constraints.
risks.title: Objective mis-specification

risks.affected_roles: Analysts, data providers, and decision makers using the model.
risks.consequence: May make estimates and plans diverge from real demand.
risks.mitigation: Perform quality checks and sensitivity analysis.
risks.title: Data bias

risks.affected_roles: Analysts, business executing parties, and decision makers.
risks.consequence: May produce an unexecutable plan that violates capacity or business conditions.
risks.mitigation: Have the executing party review the model.
risks.scenario: Capacity, regulations, or manual rules are not counted.
risks.title: Omitted constraints

risks.affected_roles: Model developers, operations teams, and plan users.
risks.consequence: May fail when demand changes and lead to misallocated resources.
risks.scenario: The model works only in historical scenarios.
risks.title: Overfitting the solution

risks.affected_roles: Analysts, managers, and teams executing the plan.
risks.consequence: May misunderstand model conditions or use results for out-of-scope decisions.
risks.scenario: Cannot explain why the plan changed.
risks.title: Black-box explanation

risks.affected_roles: Analysts, clients, data subjects, and data administrators.
risks.consequence: May expose restricted details and violate applicable contracts or data rules.
risks.mitigation: Use approved environments and de-identified samples.
risks.scenario: Client or operational details are uploaded.
risks.title: Data leakage
